title: Bureau of Future Affairs | The Interstellar Astronaut (Prequel)
subtitle: The story before Benjamin became an interstellar astronaut: humorous soft science fiction.
body:
**NOTE:** Science fiction for my own amusement. The story is now complete. (First written on 2019-12-20.)

================

## That Wretched Jump Class
“Spirits of heaven, spirits of earth, dear God, please don’t let me fail again this time.” Benjamin prayed in his grandmother’s manner. He took a deep breath and opened his midterm grade report.

Cosmic Ray Studies — A

Solar System Cosmography — A+

Origins of Cosmic Civilizations — B+

Jump Theory [Advanced] — A

Jump Practice [Elementary] — F (Please apply for a retake before next semester begins)

“No way! How did I fail again!” Benjamin’s brows knotted, and he clawed at his hair in frustrated agitation. This was already his third time taking the practical course. If he failed the retake too, he would not be able to apply for the interstellar astronautics major.

This jump-practice class really was baffling. In the three years since it had first been offered, only a dozen or so students had passed, all barely scraping through. The senior girl with the highest grade had only received a B−. According to her, she had specially gone to Russia before the exam to pay respects to Yuri Alekseyevich Gagarin, the first human in space. This successfully started a new wave of “superstition” in the aerospace college. Almost every student taking jump practice would pay respects to a relevant historical figure before the exam.

Those who could not travel to Russia visited Neil Armstrong, the first human on the Moon; the Montgolfier brothers, who gave humanity’s first public hot-air-balloon demonstration; or the Wright brothers, inventors of the airplane. Those were not too outrageous. One fellow set up a spirit tablet for Wan Hu and offered fine food and wine for a whole week before the exam. Who knows whether he had studied history badly or was deliberately going against the grain? After all, the Wan Hu he worshipped had tied forty-seven homemade rockets to a chair and held large kites in both hands, trying to fly by rocket thrust. The rockets exploded, and Wan Hu gave his life. This fellow duly failed the class all three times and, disheartened, transferred to the neighboring aerospace propulsion systems major.

Benjamin had not believed in such nonsense at first. His grades had always been excellent. Although he had long heard the pass rate was appallingly low, he enrolled without hesitation in his first year. He thought: I’ve already taught myself elementary and intermediate jump theory. Elementary jump practice should be a piece of cake! As it turned out, there was a reason a course’s pass rate was that appalling. Two months into the class, all the students were still utterly lost. Never mind judging the currently available jump-level range: most could not even tell whether a jump opportunity had appeared.

Benjamin still remembered coming out of the jump-operation simulator for the first time—face flushed, forehead slick with sweat. He had learned the theory so well, yet sitting inside the simulator he could not perform the textbook’s steps at all. Strangely, it was neither that he had forgotten them nor that he was too nervous. During those two hours in the simulator, he had not correctly identified even one jump opportunity. Every time the machine said, “A jump opportunity is about to appear; prepare to assess,” he felt nothing.

“What the hell!” A curse came from the adjacent machine too. From the sound of it, the student next door was having an equally unsuccessful practice session. Sure enough, only three of the forty students attending received passing marks that day. Of those three, only one eventually passed the final assessment.

## Strange After-Class Tutoring
“Beep—31415 requests a connection. Allow?” Tmall Genie asked in his ear.

“Allow connection.”

“Benjamin, known is that this time still you have not passed jump practice. After-class no tutoring, need?”

“Urgently needed, thanks very much!”

“Package sent. Please receive on July sixteen, year twenty-hundred-nine-one-two.”

“Thank you, 31415-kun!”

“Don’t mention it!”

After disconnecting, Benjamin could not help rolling his eyes. Tmall Genie? Tmall Idiot, more like! Next month, when his father sent his living allowance, he absolutely had to buy a new intelligent-assistant system. If he had not given in to his classmates’ urging last month and secretly gone to Hawaii for a private pilot’s license, he would not be so strapped for cash that he could not even afford an ihelp robot.

Tmall Genie was cheap, certainly, but its quality really was not great. Connecting with humans and doing simultaneous interpretation, it managed passably. The moment alien languages were involved, it fell apart spectacularly. Any fool could tell its built-in brainwave-to-soundwave conversion system had been outsourced to several different companies, and the programmer responsible for integrating them had been extremely careless. The conversion came out as a headache-inducing jumble of languages. Most infuriatingly, after every connection this idiot invariably asked, “Are you satisfied with this connection service?” Choosing “Satisfied” was fine. Choose “Dissatisfied,” and it immediately launched a purchase prompt: “Would you like to buy Tmall Genie VII? Trade in your old model for a 30% discount!”

While he was thinking about replacing his assistant, the household Google butler brought in Professor 31415’s package. Benjamin flopped onto the bed and told it, “Open it for me!”

“Certainly, Benjamin!” The Google butler rotated its palm and retracted it into its metal arm. A small knife popped out from the side and slit the outer wrapping. Carefully it lifted out the box inside. “Opening this item requires Benjamin’s own biometric information. Do you consent?” “Oh, enough. Just hand it to me!”

Benjamin sat up. What treasure had Professor 31415 put in this after-class tutoring package to make it so mysterious? He took the box from the butler and pressed his fingerprint to it. Nothing happened. How strange! He turned it over and shook it. It seemed solid: there was not the slightest sound inside.

“What is this? So weird!” He tossed the opened package onto his bed, connected Tmall Genie, and began listening to the recently popular ancient science-fiction series *Foundation*. The books were old. Although many of their author’s imaginings had now come true, their twisting, extraordinary plots kept them in the top twenty bestsellers. In particular, a recently encountered alien civilization bore an astonishing resemblance to Gaia in the books, leading countless people to wonder privately whether Asimov had been a modern person who traveled back in time years ago.

## The Amazing Cousin Is Here

“Cousin! Grandma sent your favorite salted-pork and egg-yolk zongzi. Come out and eat while they’re hot!” His younger cousin’s clear voice called from the living room.

“Okay! Coming!” Benjamin answered as he sprang off the bed.

“That was quick! Auntie said you’ve just finished this semester’s classes and have two months of summer vacation. Planning to come back to China for a few days? Grandma and Grandpa miss you.” Xu Wenxuan took the pork zongzi out of the microwave as she spoke.

“Sigh. Classes are finished, yes, but I didn’t pass the exam. I’ll have to study hard over summer for the retake. I’m afraid I won’t have time to go back to China.” Benjamin shook his head, looking troubled.

“No way. Even my genius cousin fails exams? Here, two egg-yolk zongzi. May you get a hundred on the retake!” Smiling, Wenxuan handed him the reheated zongzi. Her aunt was so thoughtful: to let Benjamin taste the food of his childhood at Grandma’s, she still kept antique appliances such as a microwave and rice cooker. They had to be used carefully every time; if these antiques broke, there really would be no one to repair them.

“Thanks, Wenxuan! These smell amazing! Exactly like the ones I used to eat at Grandma’s in Guangzhou. She’s still such a good cook! By the way, is everything sorted for your exchange at our school next semester?”

“Mostly. I packed my things in China before coming. In a couple of days they’ll all be shipped to the dorm through United Shipping.”

“United Shipping?” Benjamin raised an eyebrow. “Don’t you get seasick?”

“Of course. Also airsick, carsick, maglev-train-sick, and vacuum-elevator-sick.” Wenxuan counted on her fingers calmly. “When my parents took me out as a child, they had to give me medicine a day in advance.”

“And you still dare use sea freight?”

“My luggage is going, not me!” She rolled her eyes. “Seriously, though, even watching a video of a boat floating on the sea makes me a little nauseous. My reaction is so strong it’s hopeless.”

“It’s a wonder you’ve survived this long,” Benjamin reflected, gnawing on his zongzi.

“Thank you. I often think so too.” Wenxuan nodded earnestly.

## The Simulator and the Salted Plums

The room held only the simulator’s low hum and the occasional sound of remote-control buttons from the living room. Images of space flowed slowly across the screen like ocean waves, casting an impatient light on Benjamin’s face.

“Ugh, why is it red again!” Benjamin stared at the jump simulator as the thirteenth failure notification appeared. He gently knocked his forehead against the control panel several times, as though enough knocking could move this training device, a supreme achievement of human civilization, into becoming a gentler machine.

“Can’t you get a different one?” Wenxuan called from the living room. She was half reclining on the sofa, wrapped in an old pink blanket, watching a show and eating salted preserved plums. Beside the blanket was her usual bottle of motion-sickness medicine, kept handy for when watching too long made her dizzy.

“I’m starting to suspect the one I bought is the same defective model the professor sent me.”

“Didn’t you press ‘Confirm receipt’ three times yourself?”

“I pressed it by accident.” Benjamin was completely unabashed.

Wenxuan rolled her eyes and tossed a finished plum pit into the recycling bin beside her. “In the show they say failure is the mother of success.”

“Are we sure it isn’t the stepmother?” Benjamin muttered.

“Stepmothers can be good mothers too. What century is this? Don’t tell me you still have feudal ideas.” His cousin glared at him.

The simulator kept running. Simulated spatial curves rose and fell on the screen like ocean waves. He watched those key data points carefully, yet could never grasp the supposed “disturbance characteristics when the jump window appears.” The course’s simulated data made perfect sense in explanation, but when it came to practice, he simply could not feel it.

“Did you just say you were dizzy?”

“Hm?” Wenxuan answered indistinctly through a mouthful of plum. “A little dizzy just now. My ears felt a bit blocked… Maybe my blood sugar’s low again.”

“Did you eat earlier?”

“Yes. Two zongzi, three fish balls, and a whole bag of these.” She lifted the bag of salted plums.

“Then it isn’t low blood sugar.”

“What is it, then?”

Benjamin frowned. A vague thought suddenly crossed his mind. Instinctively he glanced at her bottle of motion-sickness medicine, then back at the failure records still flashing on the simulator. His voice slowed a little.

“Have you been getting motion sickness since you were little?”

“Terribly. Ten minutes looking out a maglev window and I throw up. Riding an autonomous bus sent me to hospital as a kid. Even those slow sightseeing boats make me horribly sick.” Wenxuan looked as though this were obvious. “That’s why I’ve never understood why you aerospace dogs insist on tormenting yourselves.”

“Then the first time you got dizzy just now—was it when I started training?”

“I think so.”

“The second was… when I adjusted the subjective sensitivity?”

“Yes.”

“And just now was the third…”

“Why are you keeping track?”

Benjamin’s lazy expression abruptly vanished. His brows drew together. He sat bolt upright, seriousness and uncertainty flashing together in his eyes. Without answering, he rapidly typed commands into the screen and pulled up the simulator’s background data. The three predicted jump-window times matched Wenxuan’s “dizziness” exactly.

He stared at the screen and sat without a word for a long time.

The fourth time: “I think I’m dizzy again.” Wenxuan frowned against the sofa.

The fluctuation curve beside the simulator flashed, and a notification sounded: jump window successfully detected.

Wenxuan only held her stomach and muttered, “Are the plums too salty… I feel a bit sick.”

Benjamin bitterly regretted his earlier choice: if only he hadn’t gone training for that pilot’s license.

---

*Translator’s note: The deliberately garbled date and mixed-language tutoring dialogue reproduce the malfunctioning translator’s speech in the original.*
